title: Return to sport following low-risk and high-risk bone stress injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Hoenig T, Eissele J, Strahl A, Popp KL, Stürznickel J, Ackerman KE, et al.
population: Athletes with lower-extremity and pelvic bone stress injuries (BSIs) in 76 studies reporting 2974 BSIs
findings: 76 studies reporting on 2974 BSIs were included; 16 compared multiple sites and 11 described anatomical site as prognostic for return to sport or complication rate.

Pooled time to return to sport was longest for tarsal navicular (127 days; 95% CI 102-151) and femoral neck (107 days; 95% CI 79-135), and shortest for posteromedial tibial shaft (44 days; 95% CI 27-61) and fibula (56 days; 95% CI 13-100).
More than 90% of athletes successfully returned to sport overall.
Complication rate was highest in BSIs of the femoral neck, tarsal navicular, anterior tibial shaft and fifth metatarsal, and lowest in the fibula, pubic bone and posteromedial tibial shaft.
limitations: Return to sport, not run-specific; heterogeneous definitions across mostly retrospective and small studies; sample size counts injuries, not people; pooled intervals for some sites are wide (e.g. fibula 13-100 days).
implications: When a BSI is logged, set the earliest return-to-run date by site: about 6 weeks (44 days) for posteromedial tibial shaft up to about 18 weeks (127 days) for tarsal navicular; these are pooled averages, so treat them as minimum planning intervals.
Treat femoral neck, tarsal navicular, anterior tibial shaft and fifth metatarsal as high-risk requiring clinician clearance; block automatic plan resumption until a clinician-cleared date is entered.
